title: Rearranging formulae
examples: How do I get y by itself in this equation?
What do I do if I have x squared on both sides?
Can you show me an example with a square root?

explain.say: Today we learn to rearrange formulae. This means we change the subject of the formula. We want to make a specific variable the subject. For example, we might want to make y the subject.

items: Make a specific variable the subject

draw.text: Rearranging Formulae: Make y the subject

explain.say: Step one is to isolate the term you want to keep. You use the inverse operation to move things across the equals sign. Remember that addition becomes subtraction. For example, if we have y plus five equals ten, we subtract five from both sides.

Step two involves dealing with multiplication and division. If a term is multiplied by a number, you divide by that number. If it is divided by a number, you multiply by it. For example, two times x equals twelve. We divide both sides by two to get x equals six.

Step three covers powers and roots. To remove a square, you square root both sides. To remove a square root, you square both sides. For example, if x squared equals twenty-five, we take the square root of both sides to find x.

faq.q: What is the first thing I should do when rearranging a formula?
faq.a: First, look at the term you want to be the subject. You need to move everything else away from it. Use inverse operations to start isolating that term.
asks: What is the first step in making x the subject?

faq.q: When I have $x$ squared, how do I get $x$ by itself?
faq.a: If you have $x$ squared, you must take the square root of both sides of the equation. Remember that taking the square root is the opposite of squaring a number.
asks: What is the inverse of squaring a variable?

faq.q: Does the order I do the steps matter?
faq.a: Yes, the order is very important. You must undo the operations in the reverse order they were applied. Think of it like unwrapping a gift.
asks: Can I do the steps in any order?
Is there a specific order for rearranging?

faq.q: What if I have fractions in the formula?
faq.a: If you have fractions, you can multiply both sides by the common denominator. This will clear the fractions and make the algebra simpler to manage.
asks: What if the equation has denominators?

faq.q: Do I change the sign when I move a term?
faq.a: Yes, when you move a term from one side to the other, you must change its sign. Addition becomes subtraction, and subtraction becomes addition.
asks: Do I change the sign when I cross the equals?
What happens to the sign when I move a term?

facts: To rearrange a formula, you must keep the equation balanced.
Inverse operations are used to move terms across the equals sign.
The inverse of squaring a variable is taking the square root.
When moving a term, its sign must change.

quiz.say: If $A = 3x + 5$ and you want $x$, what is the correct rearranged formula?
quiz.why: You correctly subtracted five and then divided by three to isolate x.

wrong.0: This incorrectly divides only five by three, leaving the A attached to the subtraction.
wrong.1: This incorrectly adds five instead of subtracting it to keep the balance.
wrong.2: This incorrectly treats the coefficients as if they were added together.

quiz.say: Rearrange the formula $V = l imes w imes h$ to make $l$ the subject.
quiz.why: You correctly divided the volume by the product of width and height.

wrong.0: This incorrectly subtracts the product of w and h from V.
wrong.1: While this looks correct, the proper way to write it clearly is using parentheses.
wrong.3: This incorrectly multiplies the result by h instead of dividing by it.
